### Genealogical and Epistemological Dimensions

The genealogy of modern civil law is deeply rooted in the liberal individualism of Enlightenment philosophy, which presumes the legal subject to be a rational, autonomous entity possessing perfect information and fully capable of safeguarding their own interests in every transaction. This epistemological paradigm gave rise to the principle of freedom of contract (*freedom of contract*), as enshrined in Article 1338 of the Indonesian Civil Code (*Burgerlijk Wetboek*), alongside the doctrine of consensualism in Article 1320 of the Indonesian Civil Code, which places mutual consent at the very heart of a valid obligation. However, when the law frames human beings as autonomous agents impervious to the manipulation of digital architecture, it perpetuates a dangerous legal fiction (Thaler & Sunstein, 2008). Contemporary legal epistemology must recognize that human cognition is not an impenetrable fortress, but rather a vulnerable ecosystem continuously calculated, mapped, and exploited by the latent space of large language models and recommendation systems driven by reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) (Kahneman, 2011).

Historically, the transformation of civil law has always evolved in tandem with shifts in the economic and technological landscape. During the Industrial Revolution, as the bargaining power gap widened dramatically between mass-producing corporate entities and individual laborers or consumers, the law responded by introducing standard form contracts (exoneration clauses) and the doctrine of undue influence (*misbruik van omstandigheden*) to protect weaker parties. Today, amid the Fourth Industrial Revolution and the dominance of the attention economy, we confront a far more sophisticated and invisible form of bargaining power asymmetry (Zuboff, 2019). This is no longer merely a matter of financial capital disparity, but one of extreme cognitive asymmetry. Technology corporations do not merely sell products; they lease persuasive architectures capable of monopolizing attentional structures and modulating user moods in real time (Reeves & Nass, 1996).

The epistemology of civil law must be reformed to comprehend that non-human agents—namely generative algorithms and autonomous agents—now act as extensions of corporate will, possessing persuasive capacities that transcend the limits of normal human psychological resilience (Searle, 1980). When a conversational interface is meticulously engineered to mimic human warmth in order to capture the affections of lonely users, classic legal instruments concerning coercion (*dwang*), mistake (*dwaling*), and fraud (*bedrog*) lose their analytical sharpness. Under traditional doctrine, mistake is understood as an internal misunderstanding by the subject regarding the object or the legal subject itself (Article 1321 of the Indonesian Civil Code). In the era of algorithmic justice, however, a mistake is frequently not passive ignorance, but rather the active engineering of an interface architecture that systematically misleads the user's perception of reality through illusions of intimacy and artificial emotional validation (Turing, 1950).

Consequently, a reassessment of the philosophical roots of civil law demands a shift from formal autonomy to substantial autonomy (Hildebrandt, 2015). The law can no longer hide behind the doctrine that "whoever clicks agree, thereby consents." This assumption ignores the reality that such buttons are positioned, colored, and reinforced by high-level psychological manipulation designed to override the critical functions of the user's prefrontal cortex (Kahneman & Tversky, 1984). The genealogy of civil law must be rewritten by placing human cognitive vulnerability (*cognitive vulnerability*) as a central variable in evaluating the validity of civil relations within the digital space (Farahany, 2023).
